etymologies.etymologyHTML: Coined between 1300 and 1350 from Middle English repairen, from Middle French reparer, from Latin reparō (“renew, repair”).

definitions.definition: To restore to good working order, fix, or improve damaged condition; to mend; to remedy.

quote.citation: 1671, John Milton, “Samson Agonistes, […].”, in Paradise Regain’d. A Poem. In IV Books. To which is Added, Samson Agonistes, London:  […]  J[ohn] M[acock] for John Starkey […], →OCLC, page 44:
quote.text: Secret refreſhings, that repair his ſtrength,

quote.citation: 1807, William Wordsworth, “To the Daisy”, in Poems, in Two Volumes, volume II, London:  […]  Longman, Hurst, Rees, and Orme, […], →OCLC, page 96:
quote.text: Do thou, as thou art wont, repair / My heart with gladness,

definitions.definition: To make amends for, as for an injury, by an equivalent; to indemnify for.

quote.citation: c. 1603–1606, William Shakespeare, “The Tragedie of King Lear”, in Mr. William Shakespeares Comedies, Histories, & Tragedies […] (First Folio), London:  […]  Isaac Iaggard, and Ed[ward] Blount, published 1623, →OCLC, [Act IV, scene i]:
quote.text: I'll repair the misery thou dost bear.

quote.citation: 2014 June 14, “It's a gas”, in The Economist, volume 411, number 8891:
quote.text: One of the hidden glories of Victorian engineering is proper drains. […] But out of sight is out of mind. And that […] means that many old sewers have been neglected and are in dire need of repair.

definitions.definition: The condition of something, in respect of need for repair.

quote.citation: 1962 March, J. M. Tolson, “The Netherlands Railways today—I”, in Modern Railways, page 172:
quote.text: The 1300 class (Nos. 1301-16), one of which was damaged beyond repair in an accident, are Co-Cos, weigh 111 tons and have a top speed of 85 m.p.h.

quote.citation: 2020 January 12, Benedict le Vay, “The heroes of Soham...”, in RAIL, number 948, page 43:
quote.text: Thirteen houses were damaged beyond repair, and much of the rest of the town suffered broken windows and lost slates.

etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English repairen (“to return”), from Old French repairier, from Late Latin repatriare (“to return to one's country”), from re- + patria (“homeland”). Cognate to repatriate.

definitions.definition: The act of repairing or resorting to a place.

quote.citation: 1702–1704, Edward [Hyde, 1st] Earl of Clarendon, “(please specify |book=I to XVI)”, in The History of the Rebellion and Civil Wars in England, Begun in the Year 1641. […], Oxford, Oxfordshire: Printed at the Theater, published 1707, →OCLC:
quote.text: The king sent a proclamation for their repair to their houses.

definitions.definition: A place to which one goes frequently or habitually; a haunt.

quote.citation: 1667, John Dryden, Annus Mirabilis: The Year of Wonders, 1666. […], London:  […]  Henry Herringman, […], →OCLC, (please specify the stanza number):
quote.text: There the fierce winds his tender force assail / And beat him downward to his first repair.

definitions.definition: To transfer oneself to another place.

quote.citation: c. 1699 – 1703, Alexander Pope, “The First Book of Statius His Thebais”, in The Works of Mr. Alexander Pope, volume I, London:  […]  W[illiam] Bowyer, for Bernard Lintot, […], published 1717, →OCLC:
quote.text: Go, mount the winds, and to the shades repair.

quote.citation: 1828, [Edward Bulwer-Lytton], chapter XVI, in Pelham; or, The Adventures of a Gentleman. […], volume I, London: Henry Colburn, […], →OCLC, page 111:
quote.text: At the hour of half-past five we repaired to our engagement.

quote.citation: 1847 October 16, Currer Bell [pseudonym; Charlotte Brontë], chapter IV, in Jane Eyre. An Autobiography. […], volume II, London: Smith, Elder, and Co., […], →OCLC, page 109:
quote.text: At a late hour, after I had been in bed some time, I heard the visitors repair to their chambers:

quote.citation: 1908, W[illiam] B[lair] M[orton] Ferguson, chapter IV, in Zollenstein, New York, N.Y.: D. Appleton & Company, →OCLC, page 47:
quote.text: That finished, I repaired to my room, one flight up, and, after a thorough wash, seated myself, pipe in mouth, at the little window that opened on the Rue Garde.

quote.citation: 1960 April, B. Perren, “Resorts for Railfans -30: Bournemouth”, in Trains Illustrated, page 239:
quote.text: [...] the train engine uncouples and either backs on to the up through line to await its next duty or repairs to the motive power depot.

etymologies.etymologyHTML: From re- +‎ pair.
